newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sits tight in late Europe, awaits G7 talks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sits tight in late Europe, awaits G7 talks.

text.p: Dollar sentiment was firm in late European trade as data depicting a tame inflation scene in Germany reduced perceptions of an interest rate hike there anytime soon.
However, operators were wary of pushing the dollar very far ahead of a Group of Seven finance ministers' meeting this weekend, and the dollar had backed off its highs against the mark by late trade.
Talks between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, scheduled for Friday, were also keeping traders' hands tied.
The dollar was at 1.7150/55 marks at 1528 GMT against 1.7125/35 in late European trade on Wednesday, after spending most of the day trapped in a very small range just below 1.72.

Dollar/mark dipped in late trade as the mark strengthened against other European currencies, the French franc in particular, on an opinion poll which highlighted French voters' doubts about European economic and monetary union.

The survey, carried out by the Louis Harris institute for Valeurs Actuelles magazine, showed 50 percent believe EMU will not help economic growth and that 69 percent favour a new referendum on the single currency.
Another opinion poll by IPSOS showed the ruling coalition was expected to win the May 25/June 1 general election by a wafer-thin majority.

When the election was called earlier this week, the French franc weakened against the mark on fears that a victory by the opposition Socialists would mean the government would have to struggle to balance its pro-EMU policies with efforts for economic growth.
However, this move on the mark crosses on Thursday did not have a heavy impact on dollar/mark and analysts were sanguine about dollar sentiment.

"It (the German inflation data) wasn't dramatic but it was pretty favourable for the dollar, with a further reduction in inflation expectations in the longer term," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International.
"When you get data from Germany indicating a fall in inflation, no one will expect rates there to go up for quite some time," he said.
West German consumer prices fell 0.1 percent on the month in April, although they rose 1.4 percent year-on-year.
The dollar was also softer against the yen after trading in a narrow range for most of the session.
It was at 125.85/95 at 1555 GMT, just off its session low, against 126.15/18 in late Europe on Wednesday.

Market operators were not taking any chances ahead of the G7 meeting and US-Japan summit, but analysts said expectations of a strongly worded statement on currencies coming out of the talks had mostly faded.

"Every time we've gone into a G7 meeting in the past, the market's been somewhat disappointed. The market's been caught out on that one so many times, it's becoming rather wary now," Yamaichi's Richardson said.

International Monetary Fund managing director Michel Camdessus said he saw no reason to be nervous about currency markets now, and added that he did not see intervention as the first order of priority now.
Camdessus also told Reuters Financial Television that the yen's current level was justified but would not be in the medium term if the Japanese economy were to strengthen further.
